base.prose: Building on this understanding, the G20 \cite{g20-2023-digital-economy-ministers} described DPI as a set of shared digital systems that should be secure and interoperable, and can be built on open standards and specifications to deliver and provide equitable access to public and/or private services at societal scale and are governed by applicable legal frameworks and enabling rules to drive development, inclusion, innovation, trust, and competition, while respecting human rights and fundamental freedoms. Taken together, these definitions establish foundational characteristics of DPI: that it is shared infrastructure operating at societal scale, and that its value derives not from any single system but from its open, interoperable nature upon which both public and private actors can build. The G20 itself recognises that DPI is an evolving concept, not necessarily limited to systems with these characteristics, and one that may be tailored to specific country contexts and referred to using different terminologies.<sup>7</sup> This provides the basis for articulating a health-specific understanding of DPI, adapted to the needs of the health sector while remaining consistent with the broader consensus. It is from this cross-sectoral understanding that health-specific digital public infrastructure is derived.

head.prose: Building on this understanding, the G20 \cite{g20-2023-digital-economy-ministers} described DPI as a set of shared digital systems that should be secure and interoperable, and can be built on open standards and specifications to deliver and provide equitable access to public and/or private services at societal scale and are governed by applicable legal frameworks and enabling rules to drive development, inclusion, innovation, trust, and competition, while respecting human rights and fundamental freedoms. Taken together, these definitions establish foundational characteristics of DPI: that it is shared socio-technical infrastructure operating at societal scale, and that its value derives not from any single system or agency asset, but from its open, interoperable, and publicly governed nature upon which public, private, and civil-society actors can build to create public value. The G20 itself recognises that DPI is an evolving concept, not necessarily limited to systems with these characteristics, and one that may be tailored to specific country contexts and referred to using different terminologies.<sup>7</sup> Complementing this consensus, the [Universal DPI Safeguards Framework](https://www.dpi-safeguards.org/framework) emphasises that DPI must be accompanied by foundational and operational safeguards — including inclusive governance, accountability, data protection, and the preservation of assisted and non-digital access routes — so that digitalisation advances inclusion and human rights rather than creating new barriers to essential services. This provides the basis for articulating a health-specific understanding of DPI, adapted to the needs of the health sector while remaining consistent with the broader cross-sectoral consensus. It is from this understanding that health-specific digital public infrastructure is derived.

base.prose: These digital resources for health — encompassing both systems and specifications — leverage foundational DPI, are interoperable, reusable, publicly governed and built on open standards. They enable countries to autonomously manage the secure processing, collection, exchange, and use of health-related data to deliver essential health services and fulfil core health sector functions, while upholding individual data rights and ensuring equitable access.

head.prose: As an evolving, publicly governed socio-technical infrastructure, these digital resources for health — encompassing shared systems, specifications, and enabling governance — leverage foundational DPI, are interoperable and reusable, and are built on open standards. They enable countries to autonomously manage the secure processing, collection, exchange, and use of health-related data to deliver essential health services and fulfil multiple health and public-health functions, creating public value across the broader health ecosystem — including people, communities, public and private providers, civil society, and subnational actors, rather than serving only central health-agency functions — while upholding individual data rights and ensuring equitable access. Consistent with the [Universal DPI Safeguards Framework](https://www.dpi-safeguards.org/framework), DPI-H is complementary to equitable assisted and non-digital access routes, ensuring that no one is excluded from care or public-health services where digital identity, literacy, connectivity, or devices are uneven.
